name: Dark Madder Violet
lede: Dark Madder Violet is a deep, greyed violet from Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature for naturalists, named for the dull red-purple of the madder dye rather than any violet pigment.

sections.title: Madder's dark cousin
sections.body:
Robert Ridgway recorded this color in 1912 as plate XXV, hue 63 prime, tone m, in his *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature*, a reference built for describing birds, insects and plants rather than paint [1]. The American ISCC-NBS dictionary later filed the same swatch as block 224, a grayish violet, and Werner's 1821 nomenclature lists a near-duplicate it calls Pale Blackish Purple, only 1.1 units away, tied to a mineral example, porcelain jasper [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[inde-blue]], [[dusky-violet]], [[dark-bluish-violet]] and [[cathedral]], at 3.3, 3.7, 3.7 and 3.7 ΔE [1]. A second Ridgway-and-ISCC-NBS near-duplicate, Dark Nigrosin Violet, sits 2.5 units off [1]. 3, 3.7, 3.7 and 3.7 ΔE [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this dark violet in 132 of 23,781 paintings, 0.56 percent, more common than 54 percent of our named colors, as photographed [2]. It most often hides in shadow, in 44 percent of its appearances, rather than reading as a mid-tone or highlight [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 20 of 1,674 paintings, three times the archive's baseline for that century [2]. The earliest dated example, from 1099, sits more than seven centuries before Ridgway's 1912 record of the name, so the match is a look-alike hue in aged, varnished paint, never proof of the madder pigment, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].

questions.q: What is Dark Madder Violet named after?
True or false: Ridgway built his 1912 nomenclature for describing paintings.

openers: Dark Madder Violet is named for a red dye plant, even though the color itself is violet.
